title: I Drove Three Hours to Surprise My Son on Thanksgiving Because for Months He Kept Making Excuses About Why I Could Not See My Fourteen-Year-Old Grandson, but as I Turned Onto His Street I Slammed on the Brakes When I Saw Ethan Standing by t
excerpt: For months, every time I asked to talk to my grandson, my son had an excuse.
author: admin

blocks.text: PART 1 — THE EXCUSES
For months, every time I asked to talk to my grandson, my son had an excuse.

My name is Margaret Sullivan. I am sixty-eight years old, a retired school librarian living in a small house in Duluth, Minnesota. My grandson Ethan is fourteen. Until last year, I talked to him every Sunday night on the phone. He told me about his science projects, his video games, the books he was reading. He was my reading buddy. We traded book recommendations like secret messages.

Ethan’s mother, my son Daniel’s first wife, passed away from an illness when Ethan was nine. For two years afterward, I drove to Minneapolis every other weekend to help. I cooked. I did laundry. I sat with Ethan while he cried.
Then Daniel remarried. Her name was Kristin. She had two young daughters of her own. And slowly, everything about my grandson went quiet.
I tried to like Kristin. At the wedding, I hugged her and told her I hoped we would be friends. She smiled and said, “Of course, Margaret.” But her eyes slid away from mine, toward the photographer.
At first the phone calls got shorter. Then they stopped coming on Sundays. Then they stopped altogether.
When I texted Ethan, he did not answer. When I called the house, Kristin usually picked up. She was always polite. Always brief.
“Ethan’s busy right now, Margaret. I’ll have him call you.”
I sent him books in the mail. I never heard whether they arrived.
By November, I had not heard my grandson’s voice in five months. So I decided I would not wait for an invitation. I would drive down for Thanksgiving and surprise them.
PART 2 — THE DRIVE
I left Duluth at nine in the morning on Thanksgiving Day.
It was bitterly cold. The radio said eight degrees in Minneapolis, with a wind chill well below zero. The highway was gray and icy.

I had a pumpkin pie on the passenger seat, wrapped in a towel. I had a bag of presents in the back. A new book for Ethan, the next one in a fantasy series he loved. A warm winter hat I had knitted in his favorite color, dark green.
My friend Agnes from church told me I was being foolish, driving three hours in that cold at my age. I told her I had driven worse roads for less important reasons.
I did not tell Daniel I was coming. I knew he would find a reason to tell me not to.
The whole three hours, I rehearsed what I would say. I’m sorry for just showing up. I won’t stay long. I just wanted to see my grandson.
I reached their neighborhood just before noon. A nice suburb with big houses and neat lawns. Snow piled along the curbs. Cars lined the street outside Daniel’s house. They had company.
I turned onto their street slowly, looking for a place to park.

Standing at the end of the driveway, beside the mailbox, was a thin boy in basketball shorts, sneakers without socks and a thin gray T-shirt. His arms were wrapped around himself. His bare legs were bright red from the cold. His breath came out in white clouds.
I slammed on the brakes so hard the pumpkin pie slid off the seat and onto the floor. I did not care. I threw open my car door and ran across the icy street toward my grandson.
PART 3 — ONE QUESTION
He looked up. His lips were trembling. His teeth were chattering so hard he could barely speak.
I pulled off my own winter coat and wrapped it around him. He was shaking all over. His skin was ice cold.
“What are you doing out here? Where is your coat?”
I rubbed his arms hard through my coat, the way my mother used to rub mine when I came in from sledding as a girl.

He looked back toward the house. Through the big front window, I could see a dining room full of people. A long table. A turkey. Kristin’s relatives laughing. Kristin’s two little girls in matching dresses. Daniel at the head of the table, carving.
“Ethan,” I said, holding his face in my hands. “I’m going to ask you one question, and I need you to tell me the truth. Why are you outside?”
He looked at me for a long moment. Then his eyes filled with tears.
“Kristin said I’m not part of the family photo,” he whispered. “She said I make the pictures look weird because I’m not really hers. She told me to go wait outside until the photographer leaves.”
“Since eleven,” he said. “She said it would only be twenty minutes. But then they started eating.”
It was ten minutes to noon. Fifty minutes in eight-degree weather in shorts and a T-shirt.
“Ethan,” I said slowly, “has this happened before?”

He did not answer. He just looked down at his red, frozen feet in his sneakers. That was all the answer I needed. I walked him to my car, put him in the front seat, turned the heater on full blast, and called my son.
PART 4 — THE PHONE CALL
Daniel answered on the fourth ring. I could hear laughter and clinking glasses in the background.
“Mom? Happy Thanksgiving. Listen, it’s not a great time.”
There was a pause. Then I watched through the windshield as my son walked to the front window of his house, still holding the carving knife, and looked out at the street.
He saw my car. He saw Ethan in the front seat, wrapped in my coat.
“Why is Ethan in your car?” he said slowly.

“Because I found him standing by your mailbox in shorts and a T-shirt in eight-degree weather,” I said. “He has been out there for almost an hour. Kristin sent him outside so he wouldn’t be in her family photo.”
“That’s not possible,” Daniel said. “Kristin said he went to his room.”
“Daniel,” I said. “Come out here. Right now. Look at your son.”
Behind him, through the window, I saw several faces at the dining table turn toward the street. Someone stood up to see what was happening.
He came out without a coat. He walked across the frozen lawn and opened the passenger door of my car. Ethan was still shaking. His legs were still bright red. His fingers were white.
Daniel knelt down in the snow beside the car and took his son’s hands.
“Buddy,” he said. “Why didn’t you come inside?”

Ethan would not look at him. “Because she’d get mad,” he whispered. “She always gets mad. And then you get mad at me for upsetting her.” Daniel stayed on his knees in the snow. He did not say anything for a very long time.
PART 5 — THE TRUTH
I did not go into that house. I could not trust myself to be polite.
Instead, I drove Ethan to a coffee shop a mile away. Daniel followed in his own car. He left without telling anyone.
We sat in a corner booth. I ordered Ethan a hot chocolate and a grilled cheese sandwich. He ate it in about four bites. He was starving.
“Ethan,” I said gently. “When did you last eat?”
Slowly, over the next hour, Ethan told us everything. Things he had never told his father, because he was afraid.

He told us that Kristin did not let him eat dinner with the family unless Daniel was home. That on nights Daniel worked late, she made dinner for herself and her daughters and told Ethan to make himself a sandwich, but the bread was often gone.
He told us that Kristin’s daughters were allowed to watch television in the living room, but that he was told to stay downstairs in the basement unless he was called.
He told us that she had taken his phone in June because she said he was “on it too much.” That she was the one who told me he was busy or asleep. That she had thrown away the books I mailed him.
